messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] command structure & adaptation params
parts:
> I realize it's now a diagonal mass matrix instead
> of varying step sizes (I'll have to change the manual
> to reflect that).

Yes, when switching to a proper metric instead of the "varying step sizes" the step-size and metric elements became identifiable and so the adaptation had to be factored. Basically the variance (or covariance for dense) is estimated using the Welford algorithm while the step-size is estimated using dual-averaging.

> But did the estimation strategy change so the dual
> averaging params are no longer relevant? If so, it
> doesn't make sense to leave them in place.

No, they're used but take default values from internal constructors. It was just odd that we exposed two of the dual-averaging parameters but not the others, so I ignored the option to set them by hand when refactoring. I'd rather we make them all available, which the subcommands would make easy. For now I'll de-neuter the two existing options on master.

>
> And it won't really be "stan" from the command line,
> but "my_model sample".
>
> The executable is just "my_model", as now, but the first
> thing it'll do is look at what the next argument is,
> which would be required to be one of the subcommands.
> That is, it should work like subcommands in git or svn.
>
> It'd also be nice to have it check options, so that
> unrecognized options are rejected.

Yup, exactly what I was thinking. But how exactly do we implement it? Right now stan::io::cmd_line is agnostic to the commands, it just accumulates them and allows the user to query but any subcommand functionality would either require listing all of the possible command/subcommand relationships in stan::io::cmd_line or changing the syntax of the arguments. For example,

1) Denote subcommands with a prefix, such as s_

my_model sample hmc s_hmc_arg1 s_hmc_arg2 da s_da_arg1

This way, as stan::io::cmd_line reads the arguments it can associate commands (unprefixed) with subcommands (everything with the prefix immediately following the unprefixed command). But it's really ugly.

2) Denote subcommands with equals

my_model sample hmc:hmc_arg1,hmc_arg2 da:da_arg1

Again, easy to parse without knowing the command/subcommand relationships. Less ugly, but still pretty ugly.

3) Denote commands as flags

my_model sample -hmc hmc_arg1 hmc_arg2 -da da_arg1

4) Lookup table after parsing:

my_model sample hmc hmc_arg1 hmc_arg2 da da_arg1

gets parsed to a list

args=[hmc, hmc_arg1, hmc_arg2, da, da_arg1]

Then you just run over the list checking against a look-up table of commands and their subcommands.

5) Lookup table before parsing:

my_model sample hmc hmc_arg1 hmc_arg2 da da_arg1

While parsing you check against the big look-up table (which would have to be stored in stan::io::cmd_line now, unless we make a big giant class just to store the info). This way you can also restrict valid subcommands to those immediately following the command.

I'm just not sure what everyone's preference is. 3 seems to be the standard SVN approach although 5 wouldn't be that hard.

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] command structure & adaptation params
parts:
I'm fine with whatever adaptation strategy works best. But we should
really have a way of determining that before making changes to core
functionality.

Also, I don't think the choice between multiple step sizes/diagonal
mass matrices in any way affects the identifiability question. The
position and energy trajectories are *in no way* changed by that
implementation choice. Any identifiability issues associated with one
implementation are every bit as present in the other; even if they're
obscured, they'll still affect the speed with which the adaptation
converges.

I do think it's important to factorize the questions of overall and
relative step size estimation, which means scaling the mass matrix so
that something (largest eigenvalue? smallest eigenvalue? trace?) is
constant.

Also, I think that even with the current strategy we're much too
sensitive to the early iterations when fitting the per-variable step
sizes. Estimates of the covariance matrix from the initial warmup
samples are garbage—they only tell you how far away you initialized
the sampler from a mode. I'd like to have the mass matrix adaptation
turned off until we have some reason to believe that things have kind
of stabilized.

Matt

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] command structure & adaptation params
parts:
> Also, I don't think the choice between multiple step sizes/diagonal
> mass matrices in any way affects the identifiability question. The
> position and energy trajectories are *in no way* changed by that
> implementation choice. Any identifiability issues associated with one
> implementation are every bit as present in the other; even if they're
> obscured, they'll still affect the speed with which the adaptation
> converges.
>
> I do think it's important to factorize the questions of overall and
> relative step size estimation, which means scaling the mass matrix so
> that something (largest eigenvalue? smallest eigenvalue? trace?) is
> constant.

This is not exactly true. The problem is that, in general, you can't scale the metric arbitrarily; only in the specific case of the explicit leapfrog integrator do you have that freedom. In that case you can perform a symplectomorphism

P = (L^{T})^{-1} p
Q = L^{-1} q

and then write the integrator in terms of P and q so that you always have (epsilon * (L^{T})^{-1}) grouped together, and you're free to exchange scales arbitrarily. Because the refactoring was meant to separate the sampling algorithm, the Hamiltonian, the integrator, and the potential such a strategy was not feasible. In particular, it wouldn't work for RMHMC and implementing it would require an architecture necessitating rewrites for each new algorithm.

That said, the only real difference in the adaptation is that an update in the metric now necessitates a corresponding update of the step size or else the acceptance rate will be off. Given the performance of your step size initialization routine, however, that's hardly a problem.

> Also, I think that even with the current strategy we're much too
> sensitive to the early iterations when fitting the per-variable step
> sizes. Estimates of the covariance matrix from the initial warmup
> samples are garbage—they only tell you how far away you initialized
> the sampler from a mode. I'd like to have the mass matrix adaptation
> turned off until we have some reason to believe that things have kind
> of stabilized.

Agreed. Implementing a better warm-up is on my very long, and rapidly growing, to-do list. Hopefully once I'm settled I'll be able to burn through a bunch of it quickly and get to the warm-up sooner rather than later.

On 4/20/13 8:20 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
...

> Basically the variance (or covariance for dense) is estimated using
> the Welford algorithm while the step-size is estimated using dual-averaging.

...

Would you mind breaking out the accumulator into its
own class for testing and re-use purposes?

Something like:

class welford_accumulator {
private:
... data to store ...
public:
welford_accumulator(double prior_count);
void add_sample(const vector& y);
long num_samples() const;
void sample_mean(vector& mu) const;
void sample_variance(vector& sigma_sq) const;
void sample_covariance(matrix& Sigma) const;
};

Can the regularization you're doing,

(N*Sigma + 5*I) / (N+5),

be coded up more efficiently by just initialzing the counters?
That is, treating it like prior data?


That's why I called 5 the prior count. I also don't know
technically if that should also be included in the N * (N-1)
adjustment for bias term -- looks like your code didn't
include it.

I think Yuanjun was using the estimator

(N*Sigma + e1*diag(Sigma) + e2*I) / (N + e1 + e2)

Any reason for the switch?

This accumulator class could be templated on the real type,
but I think we'd probably only ever use the double version.
I don't see plugging our autodif vars into it.

- Bob

Close, but the online covariance estimator isn't fully
abstracted.

1. It extends the non-trivial base class mcmc::stepsize_adapter,
which isn't relevant for a covariance estimator.

2. It also calls stepsize_adapter::init() in its init()
function and the dependency isn't relevant.

3. There's a branch on whether to do adaptation or not,
which also isn't relevant.

4. It's in the wrong namespace (stan::mcmc). for a general

What I was suggesting is pulling out just the general
functionality as outlined in the public interface above.

You would keep your covar_adapter class with the same
functionality as it has now in mcmc. But it would hold
an instance of an online covariance estimator rather than
many of the individual variables it has now.

Also, why use a separate init() function? That's what the
constructor's for and it automatically calls the parent
class init() so you don't have to code it yourself. It

parts:
I think stan::prob makes more sense than stan::math.

I'd rather not introduce multiple inheritance of
implementations if we don't have to.

I'd much rather see you just include an instance
(not a reference to an instance) as a member variable.

As a design strategy, containing is much more flexible
than inheriting because you can choose what to expose.
It does mean you need to define the
methods again where you just need to pass-through
results from the accumulator. But you probably want
to name them something different anyway.

If you do multistage warmups, you probably do NOT
want to call init() twice. Or you should at least
name it something other than init(). Maybe an
init() to do allocation, etc. and a reset()?
Then init() can call reset()?

With lots of structures in programs, it's much easier
to reason about them if they get constructed once.
It's not that expensive to construct a new object
and a lot cleaner than tweaking an existing one.
The tweak needs to be sure to clear all the state,
and if done incrementally, to insure consistency.

- Bob
